text: (a) Πρὸς αἰτίαν τινὰ κίνησιν ἔχον. Spectat hoc præcipue ad causam quæ finis est, ad quam movetur, quod ex illa ut efficiente, est. Nec bene Picus expressit, Ad ullam prorsus causam refertur; cum referri ad causam etiam dicatur, quod ad eam ut auctorem quovis modo suam refert originem, etiamsi ad eam non moveatur; ut in divinis, Filius ad Patrem ut αἰτίαν refertur (uti Græcis loqui moris est), non tamen ad ipsum moveri seu motum habere, ut πρὸς αἰτίαν (tanquam scilicet ad finem) ulli eorum ac Catholici dicant; quod non sit propter finem, sed ipse cum Patre, et Spiritu sancto unus sit omnium finis, quod una bonitas, uti et natura: idcirco dictus Greg. Theologo atque Maximo, propter se, ἀναίτιος· nullam causam aut finem habens, qui propter nos, δι' αἰτίαν· propter causam est, qua scilicet homo factus est. Castigatius ergo in theologia loquendum, ne quid inde nedum obscuritatis, sed et erroris theologorum castigatissimo Maximo, in suis de theologia accedat.
anchorLine: νησιν ἔχον (a). Τὸ δὲ μὴ οὕτως ἔχον, οὐδὲ κυρίως ὤν,
en: The editor comments on the Greek phrase 'having a motion toward some cause': this chiefly concerns the cause that is the end toward which a thing moves, since it exists from that cause as from an efficient cause. Picus did not express it well in saying 'it is referred to no cause at all', since a thing is also said to be referred to a cause when it traces its origin to it in some way, even if it is not moved toward it; as in the Godhead the Son is referred to the Father as to the cause (as the Greeks are accustomed to say), yet he is not moved toward him, nor has motion, as toward a cause in the sense of an end, in the way Catholics speak of any of them: for he is not so for the sake of an end, but with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the one end of all, as there is one goodness, as there is one nature. Hence he is called by Gregory the Theologian and by Maximus 'without cause' (anaitios), having no cause or end, in so far as he is for himself, but 'through a cause' (di' aitian), on account of the cause, in so far as he became man for our sake. One must therefore speak with more care in theology, lest any obscurity, still less any error, creep into the theology of Maximus, the most careful of theologians.

text: (b) Ζωὴν ὑφεστῶσαν οὐσιωδῶς συνυπάρχουσαν. Deerat editis illa vox συνυπάρχουσαν, cujus absentia vere obscurum Maximi capitulum reddebat, quasi et istud participium superius positum referret; diceretur­que et Vita sic subsistens Verbum gignere, seu aliquid aliud illi præstare, cum ab illo potius accipiat; a quo et procedit, ut una cum Patre ejus principio, ut docet fides catholica. Scite vero Maximus ex discretis seu notionalibus in Deo, probat conjuncta et essentialia: Verbum scilicet mente præditum, quod a Mente essentialiter subsistente (Patre scilicet) nascendo esse habeat; idemque vivere, quod Vitæ essentialiter subsistenti, Spiritui sancto, coexsistat.
anchorLine: εστῶσαν οὐσιωδῶς συνυπάρχουσαν (b), τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ
en: On the words 'Life subsisting essentially, co-existing.' The editor reports that earlier editions lacked the word synuparchousan (co-existing), without which Maximus's chapter was truly obscure, as if that participle referred back to the participle placed above; and it might then be said that Life, so subsisting, begets the Word or does something else for him, whereas he rather receives from him, from whom Life also proceeds, together with the Father, as from one principle, as the catholic faith teaches. Maximus argues skilfully from the distinct, or notional, features in God to the joint and essential ones: the Word, endowed with mind, has his being by birth from the Mind subsisting essentially (the Father), and likewise lives because he co-exists with the Life subsisting essentially, the Holy Spirit.

text: (c) Μόνου μόνος οὐσιωδῶς ἀνάρχου Λόγου γεννήτωρ. Vox ἄναρχος Græcis dubii sensus, quod et existentiam ab æterno ante omnem durationem significet, et quod nullam ab alio originem habet. Sic optime Gregorius Theologus in suis de theologia, primique ratione, etiam ἄναρχον Filium ac Verbum catholice admittit, negatque merito ratione secundi, ut nobis constet μο[...]αρχία ac beatæ Trinitatis unitas, ipsa una relatione ad unum, non quasi sint tria non coordinata. Non bene itaque mihi Picus: Solus solius origine carentis Verbi secundum substantiam genitor; quod videtur implicare in adjecto, et negare Verbi nativitatem, [...] astruit: quis enim, quove modo genitor, cujus ge-nitura omnis expers originis sit? cum nativitas et gigni, ipsa sit origo seu processio viventis a viv[...] conjuncto, etc. Non ergo totum sic theologica tractare homini non theologo. De Spiritu sancto quod loquitur Maximus, omnium communiter Græcorum est: qui tamen caute terminum excludentem [...] apponunt processioni Verbi a parte principii, [...] μόνος Λόγου γεννήτωρ, nunquam vero processioni Spiritus sancti: ut nulla sit nostra, Græcorumque olim discordia, sed quam deinceps animorum contentio invexit, aliis impugnantibus, quod illi explicationis causa addendum sibi indulserunt.
anchorLine: σιωῶς ἀνάρχου Λόγου Γεννήτωρ (c)· καὶ μόνης
en: On the words 'sole father, in his essence, of the sole unoriginate Word.' The Greek word anarchos is ambiguous: it can mean existence from eternity before all duration, and also having no origin from another. So Gregory the Theologian in his theological works rightly allows the Son and Word to be 'without beginning' in the first sense and rightly denies it in the second, so that the monarchy and unity of the blessed Trinity stand clear. The editor therefore finds Picus's gloss, 'sole begetter of the Word who has no origin, according to substance', poor: it seems self-contradictory and to deny the Word's birth, which Picus himself asserts; for who, and how, is a begetter whose begetting is wholly without origin, since birth and being begotten are themselves the origin or procession of a living thing from a living thing joined to it? One should not treat theology so loosely, if one is no theologian. As for what Maximus says of the Holy Spirit, it is common to all the Greeks, who nevertheless take care to add the exclusive term 'only' to the procession of the Word from the principle, never to the procession of the Spirit, so that there is no discord of ours; the long-standing Greek discord, which later strife of minds introduced, arose when others objected to what the Greeks allowed themselves to add for explanation. (Some line-ends in this note are inked over and are marked [...].)

text: (d) Καὶ ἔτι μᾶλλον τῆς καθ' ὑπερουσιότητα θέσεως, ἀπείρως ἐξηρημένος. Significant hæc divinam eminentiam, separatione ac singularitate supra res omnes, omnemque earum positionem, seu affirmantem conceptum. Id enim illud ἐξηρημένως, qua voce in hunc sensum sæpius utitur Dionysius. Eminet ergo infinite, ab omnique secretus superessentiali positione; omni scilicet affirmatione nostra de superessentiali essentia ac natura. Paulo rudius Picus: Imo potius a thesi substantiam excedenti distat infinite.
en: On the Greek words 'and still more than the positing in the manner of super-essentiality, infinitely removed.' These words signify the divine eminence, set apart and singular above all things and above every positing of them, that is, every affirmative concept. For that is what the word exeremenos means, which Dionysius often uses in this sense. So God is infinitely eminent and set apart from every super-essential positing, namely from all our affirmation about the super-essential essence and nature. Picus, a little more crudely: 'Rather, he is infinitely distant from a positing that surpasses substance.' (Legibility note: the second instance of the Greek participle is blurred; read as ἐξηρημένως.)

text: (f) Ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων. Quod paulo ante legerat Picus, ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων, fallentibus oculis ac præcurrente calamo, hic legit ac reddidit, pro hominibus; etsi illius Græca perinde habeant ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον, supra hominem: quod unum aptum est. Est enim ratio cur ignotum et abstrusum semperque myste-rium incarnationis mysterium; quod scilicet div[...] altiorisque ordinis est, non pro humana ratione.
anchorLine: διὰ παντὸς ἔχων ἀνέκφαντον· ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον (f) γὰρ
en: On 'huper anthropon'. The editor says that Picus, who a little before had read 'huper anthropon' (for men), with deceived eyes and a hurrying pen, here read and rendered 'for men', although the Greek of the passage, in both places alike, has 'huper anthropon' (above man, beyond man): that alone fits. For there is a reason why the mystery of the incarnation is always unknown and hidden: that it is divine and of a higher order, not for human reason. text: (g) Ἡ τῶν ἁγίων δυσπάθεια. Sensus Maximi est, ea pugna vitii ac virtutis, quasi durari qui serio virtutis cultores sint, ut non facile lædi a vitio possint. Hæc enim vis ejus vocis, ut hic Maximo usurpatur, cujus significationis exstant exempla apud Bud. et Henr. Stephan. Nihil ad rem quod reddit Picus, Repugnantia affectuum quæ est in sanctis: quem sensum vox illa non partitur. Posset quidem reddi, Molestia, labor, etc., ut cap. 19 et 21; sed minus quadrat pro Maximi hic instituto. Quod in fine cap. est, Τῆς δὲ, ὅπως κατάσχῃ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς, κἂν ταῖς συμφοραῖς τὸ πλέον ἔχοντας, misere depravat idem Picus, dum ita reddit: Hæc autem, ut bonos et locupletiores in calamitatibus contineat. Plene vult Maximus, continere virtutem in officio probos, quorum etiam in ærumnis partes potiores sunt: Melior longe conditio quam malorum. Dicamus nos, Qui ont l'avantage même dans les afflictions, etc. Hæc nimirum evangelica promissio: Centies tantum nunc in tempore hoc, cum persecutionibus, Marc. x, 30; quod egregie Maximus dicit, κατορθοῦντας κολάζεσθαι, idcirco puniri malisque affici, quod virtutem colamus, et officii tenaces simus. Id certe qui præstent, inque illis patientiam teneant, seu etiam gaudeant, virtute adulti ac Christiana fortitudine, omnium vere beatissimi, adversumque omnes τὸ πλέον ἔχοντες. Rem Maximus magis explicat sequenti cap. cujus in fine aurea sententia est, Ῥῶσις ψυχῆς τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν, ὁ τοῦ σώματος αἰκισμός: Robur animi per patientiam, injuria ac sugillatio corporis.
anchorLine: δυσπάθεια (g) · τοῦ μὲν, ὅπως κρατήσῃ φιλονει-
en: On 'the impassibility (dyspatheia) of the saints.' The editor explains that Maximus means that, in the struggle of vice and virtue, those who are earnestly devoted to virtue are as if hardened, so that they cannot easily be harmed by vice; this is the force of the word as Maximus uses it here, and examples of that sense are found in Budaeus and Henri Estienne. What Picus gives, 'the conflict of the affections that is in the saints', is beside the point, since the word does not bear that sense; it could be rendered 'trouble, toil' (as in chapters 19 and 21), but that suits Maximus's purpose here less well. The editor also says Picus wrongly renders the final clause of the chapter ('that he may hold the good, even in misfortunes having the advantage'), as if it meant 'that he may keep the good and the richer in calamities'; Maximus fully intends to keep the upright in their duty, whose lot even in hardships is the better one, or who rejoice, grown strong in virtue and Christian fortitude, the most blessed of all and having the advantage over all adversaries. The editor suggests the gospel promise (a hundredfold 'now in this time, with persecutions', Mark x, 30), which Maximus states well in saying that those who do right are punished and afflicted because they cultivate virtue and hold to duty; and Maximus explains the matter further in the next chapter, whose last line is a golden saying: 'strength of soul for those who endure: the scourging of the body.' (This quoted saying is rendered in the note itself as 'robur animi per patientiam, injuria ac sugillatio corporis'.) The note also includes a French phrase, 'Qui ont l'avantage même dans les afflictions', cited from a translation.
